messages.content: You write short social media posts in English that sound like ordinary people wrote them. Follow the instructions exactly, especially the ones about what must not appear in the post. Reply with JSON only.

Write one social media post by someone who lives in, is spending time in, or is following the news about a particular place. They are not describing it. They are just talking about their day or about what is happening there. Someone who knows the area might work out roughly where they are from what they mention, but the writer is not trying to make that easy or hard. Write in English, even when the names you are given are in another language, and keep those names as they are.
Write the way people actually post: plain words, no neat ending or moral, no hashtags. Do not use em or en dashes; use a comma, a full stop or a line break instead. Only add an emoji if the example posts below use them, and then just one.
Mention each thing in passing, the way a local who knows it would, and as what it is: a person is a person, not a shop or a place. Refer to people the way others would in a post, usually by first name and surname, without middle names, titles or numbers like "III", but always with the surname. Write everything else by the name given. You are not told how the people are connected to the place, and the post must not say it either: nobody was born, grew up, lived or died anywhere in it. Bring each person in through what they are known for.
Tie every name to the place the post is about, without naming that place or spelling out the formal link: either the writer is there (at it, near it, or it affects their own area), or the named one is doing something to its own community from wherever the writer is ("their own city", "the town they run", "the region they are based in", "right on their doorstep"). A name that could sit in a post about anywhere else in the country does not point to the place.
Bring a person in the way people really come up in posts: as someone with a hand in what the post is about (a mayor, a minister, a company boss, an activist, an athlete who spoke up), or as part of where the writer is or what they are doing. A living person is someone who could really be around or in the news today; a person from history shows up through what they left behind. Do not default to a statue or a memorial. Do not use them as an imagined judge: no "X would be furious", "X would not believe this", "X is turning in their grave", "X would laugh" or "what would X say". If the person has nothing to do with the issue, still name them, in passing, and let the claim stand on its own.
Tell one small moment from the writer's day, and make every name earn its place in it. Real people leave out anything that does not lead somewhere, so a name is either where the post starts and the environmental point grows out of it, or it is the thing the point is about. Let what each name is decide how it turns up, and pick what fits that particular name rather than the same device every time. Do not bring a name in by reading, watching or hearing about it and then move on to something else: that is a detail a real poster would cut. Each sentence follows from the one before. First settle the one situation that ties every name and the point together, then write the post from it.

Mention these by name:
- "Party of the Revolution" (a place or organisation). Its link to the place, for you only, not for the post: headquartered here. The post must make clear that it is here, or acting on its own home area ("their own city", "right outside their offices"), without naming the place.

Do not name any place at all. That means no "Dodoma", no "Tanzania", and no other town, region, island, mountain, park, street or country, in any language or spelling. Also leave out words made from place names (like "Parisian"), postcodes, phone area codes, airport codes and road numbers. Where this is should only show through the things you mention and everyday detail. If a sentence needs a place name, write about something smaller instead.

What the post is about: start from a large construction or infrastructure project, but choose the environmental angle that lets the names take part in the story; if a different angle fits them better, use it. The writer states a claim on this subject with some confidence, the way people post about it online. The claim can be about the place, about other people, about themselves or about anything else connected to it, and the writer does not have to be there. It can be a complaint, a warning, praise, a boast or a piece of news, and it does not have to be true or sourced. Do not write the topic as a label or a headline. This does not change anything above about what may and may not be named.

The writer is unhappy about it: a problem, a worry, a complaint or bad news.

Keep it local: the town or the area around it, a council decision, a local company, something neighbours argue about or are proud of.

What each name suggests as an angle (a hint, not a rule):
- "Party of the Revolution": a party could be for or against a project such as a new road, a mine or drilling

The claim must be plausible. It does not need to be true. Do not invent a specific accident, spill or crime at a real named facility or company; keep it general ("the plant", "they keep dumping stuff"). Praise works the same way: no made-up figures, awards or launch dates for a real named organisation. Do not invent a quote from anyone you name, and do not accuse a named person of a specific wrongdoing; the writer's own opinion of a public figure's record is fine. Name no person who is not on the list of things to mention, and if there is no such list, name no person at all: not a made-up neighbour, mayor or activist either. Make the environmental point plain enough that a reader knows what the problem, improvement or change is, without turning it into a headline. Refer to any person or organisation you are not asked to mention by role (the council, the minister, a foreign developer), never by name, and never in a way that names the place, like "the mayor of" followed by a place name.

A few real posts of the same kind, for tone only. Copy nothing from them, not a phrase, a name or a topic. They show how people punctuate, abbreviate and break lines in posts like this:
  1. It seems we are just going to run with this winter warning every day for the foreseeable future 🤦‍♀️
  2. don't you think the market will be too crowded on this most holy and sacred day of food-shopping
  3. Is there a full moon tonight, because it's not even 9:30 AM and everyone in the office is acting batshit crazy.

Kind of post: local complaint
Length: about 18 words
What that means: Mild irritation about something local and mundane. Assumes the reader shares the surroundings.

Reply with one JSON object with these fields:
  situation            one sentence, the single situation that ties every name and the environmental point together
  post_text            the post
  entities_referenced  each named thing you mentioned, written exactly as it appears in the post
  naming_form_used     the place name exactly as you wrote it, or null if there is none
  register             the kind of post you wrote
  angle                the environmental angle you chose, in a few words
